definition.text: A structured summary of all the research on a clearly stated question, using explicit methods to find, select and judge the studies.

facts.text: Systematic reviews, sometimes with meta-analyses, are generally ranked as the highest level of evidence in scientific and medical research.
They aim to be rigorous and transparent so that bias in the findings can be assessed and, where possible, reduced.
Besides medicine, they are used for environmental and social interventions, policy reviews and economic evaluations.
Main stages: define an answerable question and publish a protocol, search sources against set criteria, extract data, judge eligibility, then analyse and combine the results.
Unlike a narrative literature review, it follows explicit, pre-stated methods.
The PRISMA statement standardizes how reviews are reported and is required by more than 170 medical journals worldwide.
Systematic reviews were sporadic until the 1980s and common after 2000; more than 10,000 are now published each year.
In social science the Campbell Collaboration's procedures are the quasi-standard, and the method is spreading to international development research.

definition.text: A statistical method that pools quantitative results from many independent studies of the same question.

facts.text: Its core step is computing one combined effect size across all the studies.
Combining studies improves statistical power and can resolve disagreements between individual studies.
It is often part of a systematic review, which assembles the studies a meta-analysis then analyses.

definition.text: A review that maps the concepts, language and data around a topic, refining its search as it goes, to gauge how much evidence an area holds.

facts.text: It often comes before a systematic review, to judge whether a full review is possible or worthwhile.
Its methods may change during the work, sometimes departing from the original protocol.
A related mapping review or systematic map sorts existing literature by quantity, quality and study design to show where more research is needed.

title: Limitations of systematic reviews
article: Systematic review#Out-dated or risk of bias

definition.text: The ways systematic reviews can mislead, through biased inputs, outdated searches or poor reporting, despite being treated as the strongest evidence.

facts.text: A 2003 review of 300 studies found systematic reviews were not all equally reliable.
Of 100 reviews monitored, 7% needed updating on publication, another 4% within a year and another 11% within 2 years.
Around half of clinical trials never report results, and 'positive' trials were twice as likely to be published as 'negative' ones, skewing what reviews can find.
Many reviews comply poorly with reporting guidelines and have weak, hard-to-reproduce search strategies.

definition.text: A forest planted to produce large volumes of wood, usually as a single-species monoculture.

facts.text: Managed timber forests commonly yield 1 to 3 cubic meters of wood per hectare per year, while fast-growing plantations commonly yield 20 to 30 or more.
In 2000 plantations made up 5% of global forest but supplied an estimated 35% of the world's roundwood.
Industrial plantations are large, even-aged blocks of one or two species, often bred for fast growth and pest resistance.
Trees are usually harvested after 10 to 60 years, so plantations lack the growth, soil, wildlife and decaying dead wood of old-growth forest.
Fast-wood plantations or fiber farms, started in Brazil in the 1970s, run on rotations as short as 5 to 15 years.
Eucalyptus is the most widely planted plantation tree worldwide.
Long-term carbon storage depends on what happens to the harvested wood.
Fiber plantations offer local people a much narrower range of services than the natural forest they replace, sometimes ignoring local rights.

title: Plantations and natural forest loss

definition.text: The argument over whether high-yield plantations spare natural forests from logging or instead replace them.

facts.text: In principle plantations need less land for the same wood; in New Zealand 19% of the forest area supplies 99% of industrial roundwood.
According to the FAO, about 7% of natural closed forest lost in the tropics is converted to plantations, and 93% to agriculture and other uses.
An estimated 15% of plantations in tropical countries are set up on closed-canopy natural forest.
Using plantations to cut carbon dioxide is challenged because the stored CO2 is eventually released after harvest.

contested_note: Foresters say plantations reduce pressure on natural forest, while in practice some plantations replace it.

title: Introduced species in plantations

definition.text: Planting tree species far outside their natural range because they grow fast and suit industrial use.

facts.text: Globally, 44 percent of plantation forests are made up mainly of introduced species.
Introduced species dominate planted forests in South America (88%), Oceania (75%) and East and Southern Africa (65%), but are only 1%, 3% and 8% in North America, West and Central Asia, and Europe.
Pine, spruce and eucalyptus are the classic examples, valued for fast growth and tolerance of degraded farmland.
